docs.title: UiPath Coding Agents Workshop
docs.text:
Build UiPath agents and Maestro orchestrations with coding agents — from installing the tools to shipping a long-running automation.

Training Environment

Log in at https://cloud.uipath.com/tpenlabs using tenant InvokeWorkshop.

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text:
This workshop takes you from zero to building real automation with coding agents. You start by setting up the uip CLI and UiPath skills, then build agents and orchestrations — letting a coding agent like Claude Code do the heavy lifting while you stay in control.

The course has two parts:

Part 1 · Coding Agents — get your environment ready, learn how building UiPath components changes with a coding agent, and build your first agents: a low-code hello-world, a coded agent with context and tools, and a conversational agent.

Part 2 · Agentic Orchestration — orchestrate agents, robots, and people into Maestro solutions: Case Management, BPMN, and Flow.

Agenda — How the hands-on session runs, in two 90-minute blocks. Finish Setup before the first block.

Hands-On Session — The recruitment pipeline you'll build: a Coded Agent, an RPA workflow, and a Maestro Flow, step by step.

More exercises are being authored and will appear here as they are released.

docs.title: Key concepts
docs.text:
• Coding agent — an AI assistant (e.g., Claude Code) that builds UiPath components from your instructions, using the uip CLI and UiPath skills. UiPath is the automation platform that coding agents operate natively.
  • uip CLI — the command-line interface coding agents use to talk to the UiPath platform.
  • UiPath skills — curated instruction packs that teach a coding agent how to build UiPath automations correctly.
  • Maestro — UiPath's orchestration platform for coordinating humans, robots, and AI agents across long-running processes.

docs.title: Coding Agents + UiPath: Hands-On Session
docs.text: Build a Coded Agent and an RPA workflow, then orchestrate them with a human approval in Maestro — the whole recruitment pipeline, in two 90-minute blocks.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Every week a recruiter at a staffing agency does the same three things by hand: write a description for each open role, read through a candidate pool to find who fits, and register the shortlist in the client's portal. Hours of work, done differently by every recruiter, with no record of who approved what.

You'll automate all three — by describing what you want in plain English and letting your coding agent build it. Two components do the work, and one Maestro flow connects them, with the recruiter still making the final call.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
By the end of the session you'll start one Maestro run with a job title and watch it end with approved candidates registered on UiBank. Along the way you'll have generated a Python agent, an XAML workflow, and a Maestro Flow — all by prompting a coding agent, not by dragging activities onto a canvas.

Training Environment

Log in at https://cloud.uipath.com/tpenlabs using tenant InvokeWorkshop.

docs.title: What You'll Build
docs.text:
Three labs, one pipeline:

  1. Coded Agent (Block 1) — a Python LangGraph agent that takes a job title, generates a structured job description, scores a candidate pool against it, and returns the top 3 matches
  2. RPA Workflow (Block 2) — a Studio XAML workflow that takes a list of candidates, registers each one on the UiBank web form, and returns a status per candidate
  3. Maestro Flow (Block 2) — a UiPath Flow that runs the agent, creates an approval task in Action Center for the recruiter, and on approval runs the RPA workflow with the shortlist

Why this architecture

Maestro passes the data from one step to the next, so there's no database to set up and no custom app to build. The recruiter reviews the shortlist in an Action Center task — the review screen comes with the platform. That's what lets the full pipeline, orchestration included, fit in 180 minutes.

docs.title: The scenario
docs.text:
A staffing agency is digitizing its recruitment pipeline. Shortlist candidates, keep a human in the loop, register the approved ones — one process, end to end. 01 Coded Agent Turns a job title into a structured JD and scores a candidate pool against it. → Returns the top 3 matches 02 RPA Workflow Registers each candidate it receives on uibank.uipath.com/register-account. → Returns a status per candidate 🔗 03 Maestro Flow Runs the agent, waits for the recruiter's approval in Action Center, then runs the robot. → One run, end to end

How the data moves through one run:

job_title
   │
   ▼
[ Coded Agent ] ──▶ job + top 3 matches
                          │
                          ▼
              [ Approval task in Action Center ]
                          │  approved
                          ▼
              [ RPA Workflow on UiBank ] ──▶ status per candidate
                          │
                          ▼
                     flow output

  All three steps run inside one Maestro Flow.

docs.title: The contract between the components
docs.text:
You build the three pieces in separate labs, so agree on the data shapes first. Every prompt below uses these names — keep them exactly as written and the Maestro lab becomes wiring, not debugging.

Component Input Output Coded Agent job_title (string) job (object) and matches (array of 3 candidates, each with all original fields plus score and reason) RPA Workflow in_CandidatesJson (string — a JSON array of candidates) out_ResultsJson (string — a JSON array of { username, status }) Maestro Flow job_title (string) the job and out_ResultsJson

Why the matches keep every candidate field

The robot needs the date of birth, title, email, and the rest to fill in the UiBank form. If the agent returns only names and scores, Lab 3 breaks. That's why the Lab 1 prompt says it explicitly.

Three things the robot needs to know about this data

  • An empty middle_name is valid. The form should skip the field, not type an empty string.
  • The date format is MM/DD/YYYY, which matches the form's picker.
  • All test passwords are demo-grade. In production, pull them from a vault.

docs.title: Lab 1 — the Coded Agent
docs.text:
Job description + candidate shortlist

Block 1 · 50 min build + 10 min checkpoint

Minutes What you do 0–5 Save candidates.json, start your coding agent in that folder, paste the prompt. 5–30 Answer its questions and let it build. Read What's a Coded Agent? while it works. 30–40 Run the agent locally and check the output against the contract. 40–50 Publish the agent as a process in the CodingAgentsILT folder. 50–60 Checkpoint with the group.

docs.title: What's a Coded Agent?
docs.text:
Python agents that run on UiPath infrastructure. Not to be confused with the coding agent you're typing into — you write this one yourself.

You pick the framework, use the UiPath SDK, package it with one CLI command, and deploy it to Orchestrator.

SUPPORTED FRAMEWORKS LangGraph Graph-based, stateful agent flows LlamaIndex RAG and document-grounded agents OpenAI Agents SDK OpenAI's official agent framework Plain Python Simple function-based agents

docs.title: What the hiring agent does
docs.text:
The four steps run in order — each one feeds the next, and Return hands the shortlist to whoever called the agent. In Lab 3, that's your Maestro Flow.

WHAT THE AGENT DOES Input 01 Take a job title, for example "Forward Deployed Engineer" Generate 02 Structured job description: title, level, must-haves, nice-to-haves Match 03 Score every candidate in the pool against the JD, with a reason Return 04 Output the JD and the top 3 matches, in the contract's shape YOUR OBJECTIVES
  • 1 Prompt your coding agent to scaffold a LangGraph agent.
  • 2 Use the UiPath LLM Gateway for the model calls, so you don't need your own API key.
  • 3 Run it locally and check the output matches the contract.
  • 4 Publish it as a process in the CodingAgentsILT folder, so Maestro can call it.
WHAT YOU NEED
  • candidates.json — see The candidate pool.
  • A logged-in uip CLI session. No personal LLM API key needed.

docs.title: The prompt
docs.text:
This is real text you can paste:

Build a UiPath Coded Agent in LangGraph called {YourName}JobMatchingAgent,
in a new folder named {YourName}JobMatchingAgent.

Input: { "job_title": string }. Output: { "job": object, "matches": array }.

1. Write a JD for the job title with 3-5 role-specific must-have skills
2. Score each candidate in candidates.json (copy it into the project) from
   0 to 100. A headline matching the job title counts most, then skills
   matching the must-haves
3. Return the JD as "job" and the top 3 as "matches", highest first. Each
   match keeps all original candidate fields, plus "score" and "reason"

Use the UiPath LLM Gateway at temperature 0, no external API keys. Add 3
evals that check the candidate whose headline matches the job title ranks
first.

Why the prompt is this specific

Fixed input and output names, a provided candidate pool, no database. Every constraint you add removes a question the agent would otherwise ask — or a decision it would make on its own. That's what keeps this lab inside 50 minutes, and what makes Lab 3 plug together.

Why the prompt sets a scoring rule

Without one, the agent writes a fresh JD on every run — often with generic must-haves like "cloud platforms" — and scores only against that JD. The same candidate can come first in one run and third in the next. The scoring rule ties the score to the job title and to concrete skills, and the evals check who ranks first, so an unstable ranking fails instead of slipping through. Expect small score changes between runs — that's normal for an LLM — but the top candidate should stay put.

WHAT THE CODING AGENT DOES WITH THAT
  • 1 Loads the uipath-agents skill.
  • 2 Generates main.py with the graph, and Pydantic models for the input, the JD, and the matches.
  • 3 Creates evals/ with three cases.
  • 4 Asks you to review before publishing.

docs.title: What it generates
docs.text:
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph
from pydantic import BaseModel

class Input(BaseModel):
    job_title: str

class Output(BaseModel):
    job: JobDescription
    matches: list[Match]          # all candidate fields + score + reason

def generate_jd(state):
    # LLM Gateway call -> structured JD
    ...

def match_candidates(state):
    candidates = load_json("candidates.json")
    # LLM Gateway call -> score every candidate, keep the top 3
    ...

graph = StateGraph(State, input=Input, output=Output)

Treat this as the shape to expect, not the exact code. Your agent's version will differ — that's fine, as long as the input and output names match the contract.

docs.title: While it builds
docs.text:
Your coding agent takes several minutes to write and check its work. Use that time:

  • Watch what it writes. Does the output keep every candidate field? Push back early — it's cheaper than after all the code exists.
  • Read What's a Coding Agent? and spot the moment it loads the uipath-agents skill.
  • When it asks a question, answer briefly and specifically. "Yes, return all original fields" beats "whatever you think".

docs.title: Run it locally
docs.text:
When your coding agent asksManual run

Your coding agent may ask if you want to run the agent locally to test it — answer yes. It starts the Developer Console on your machine and gives you a localhost link to open in your browser, like this:

http://localhost:8080/?token=••••••••••••••••

Open the full link your coding agent gives you — the token at the end is unique to your session, so don't share it. Then:

  1. Choose Autonomous.
  2. In Input, enter { "job_title": "Forward Deployed Engineer" }.
  3. Select Execute, and watch each node run.
  4. When the run completes, the right-hand panel shows the output: the JD and the three matches.

Didn't get asked, or want to run it again? Give this prompt to your coding agent:

Run the {YourName}JobMatchingAgent coded agent locally with this input:
{ "job_title": "Forward Deployed Engineer" }
Show me the output.

Core goal done

You get a JD and three matches, highest score first, with the candidate whose headline is Forward Deployed Engineer on top. Each match has a score, a reason, and every field from candidates.json — including date_of_birth and password. Publish next.

Someone else came first?

Based on candidates.json, Alice Nguyen should be the first result — she's the only candidate whose headline is Forward Deployed Engineer. If she isn't, read the reason for each match, then ask your coding agent why Alice Nguyen isn't first and to fix the scoring. Run the eval set to check the fix.

docs.title: Publish the agent
docs.text:
Maestro calls processes, not local code, so the agent has to land as a process in the CodingAgentsILT folder. Both paths do the same thing. Run the commands yourself if you want to see each step, or hand the whole job to your coding agent.

ManuallyUsing Your Coding Agent

This assumes the uip CLI is installed and you're logged into the right org. Replace the project path and tenant name with your own.

# 1. Go to the agent project
cd {YourName}JobMatchingAgent

# 2. Point the UiPath wrapper at the Python runtime
uip codedagent setup --force

# 3. Select the target tenant
uip login tenant set InvokeWorkshop --output json
uip login status --output json

# 4. Initialize the coded agent project
uip codedagent init

# 5. Publish to the tenant feed
uip codedagent deploy --tenant

Then, in Orchestrator, open the CodingAgentsILT folder and add a process from your {YourName}JobMatchingAgent package.

Give this prompt to your coding agent — it initializes the project, publishes, and creates the process for you:

Publish the {YourName}JobMatchingAgent coded agent to the CodingAgentsILT
folder, and create its process in the CodingAgentsILT folder.

Watch what it runs

The agent proposes each command before running it. Read them — publishing writes to your tenant, and that is the one step you want to see before it happens.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
Ten minutes, as a group, before the block ends:

  • Two or three people show their matches for "Forward Deployed Engineer". Did the agents agree? Why not?
  • Everyone confirms their process shows up in the CodingAgentsILT folder.
  • Didn't make it? No problem — in Lab 3 you'll use the trainer's DemoJobMatchingAgent, which follows the same contract.

docs.title: Lab 2 — the RPA Workflow
docs.text:
Register candidates where there's no API

Block 2 · 30 min

Minutes What you do 0–5 Start your coding agent in your workshop folder and paste the prompt. 5–15 Let it discover the project and generate the workflow. 15–25 Run it with the test input and watch the browser fill in the form. 25–30 Publish it as a process in the CodingAgentsILT folder.

On a Mac?

Studio Desktop runs on Windows only. Pair with someone on Windows for this lab. In Lab 3 you can use the trainer's DemoRegisterInUiBank process, which follows the same contract.

docs.title: Why RPA for this part?
docs.text: UiBank exposes registration only through a web form. There's no API. Some systems only have a UI — this is exactly what RPA was built for. RPA is the right tool Browser-based UI automation is faster and more reliable than scraping. Generated, not drawn You'll prompt your coding agent to build the XAML. No dragging activities onto a canvas. Built for Maestro Takes the shortlist as an argument and returns a status per candidate.

docs.title: What the workflow does
docs.text:
WHAT THE WORKFLOW DOES Receive 01 Parse in_CandidatesJson into a list of candidates Loop 02 For each candidate, open the registration page Fill 03 Type each field, submit, wait for success Return 04 Output out_ResultsJson with a status per candidate YOUR OBJECTIVES
  • 1 Prompt your coding agent to generate the XAML workflow.
  • 2 Let it discover the project first, so it sees the existing packages.
  • 3 Run it with the test input and check out_ResultsJson.
  • 4 Publish it as a process in the CodingAgentsILT folder.
Your target: uibank.uipath.com/register-account, the test input below, and UiPath Studio Desktop with the default packages.

docs.text:

docs.title: The prompt
docs.text:
Build a UiPath workflow project called {YourName}RegisterInUiBank, in a new
folder named {YourName}RegisterInUiBank, that registers candidates at
uibank.uipath.com/register-account.

Arguments:
  in_CandidatesJson (In, String): a JSON array of candidates with first_name,
    last_name, middle_name, sex, title, employment_status, date_of_birth,
    marital_status, num_dependents, username, email, and password. Other
    fields may be present - ignore them.
  out_ResultsJson (Out, String): a JSON array of { username, status } where
    status is Registered or Failed.

UiBank rejects a username or email it has seen before. For each candidate,
add _{yourname} and the current time (HHmmss) to the end of the username and
to the part of the email before the @ - for example alice.nguyen_maria143205
and alice.nguyen_maria143205@example.com. Then skip middle_name when it's
empty, submit, and wait for the success message. Wrap each registration in a Try/Catch so
one failure doesn't stop the run.

Use the contents of test-input.json (in this folder) as the default value
of in_CandidatesJson, so the workflow runs on its own. Inspect the project
before you write the workflow.

docs.title: How the workflow skill thinks
docs.text:
The uipath-rpa skill is discovery-first. It reads before it writes:

Let me inspect the project first...
  -> Reading project.json
  -> Found packages: UiPath.UIAutomation.Activities,
     UiPath.WebAPI.Activities

I'll create Main.xaml with:
  - Arguments in_CandidatesJson (In) and out_ResultsJson (Out)
  - Deserialize JSON Array -> candidates
  - For Each candidate
  - Open browser at registration URL
  - Type Into each form field (skip empty middle name)
  - Click Submit, wait for success element
  - Try/Catch per candidate, add { username, status } to results
  - Serialize results -> out_ResultsJson

Created Main.xaml (validated)

Four things worth noticing in that output:

Reads first 01 Discovers packages before writing any code. Picks the right activities 02 Reaches for JSON and UI Automation activities it knows exist. Handles edge cases 03 Empty middle name skipped, one failure doesn't stop the run. Honours the contract 04 Arguments named exactly as Maestro will pass them.

docs.title: Run it locally
docs.text:
Give this prompt to your coding agent:

Run {YourName}RegisterInUiBank locally with its default input and show me
out_ResultsJson.

Prefer to watch it step by step? Open the project in Studio Desktop and press Run — the test input is already set as the default.

Core goal done

The browser registers all three candidates and out_ResultsJson shows a status for each one.

docs.title: Publish the workflow
docs.text:
Give this prompt to your coding agent:

Publish {YourName}RegisterInUiBank to the InvokeWorkshop tenant and
make it available as a process in the CodingAgentsILT folder. Confirm
`uip login status` first. Report the process name, and stop if any step fails.

Then move straight on to Lab 3 — don't polish this workflow past the time box.

docs.title: 🔗 Lab 3 — the Maestro Flow
docs.text:
Agent, human, robot — one process

Block 2 · 50 min

Minutes What you do 0–5 Start your coding agent in your workshop folder and paste the prompt. 5–25 Review the flow it proposes, let it build, validate, and publish. 25–40 Run the flow, approve the task in Action Center, watch the robot register the candidates. 40–50 Fix what broke and run it again.

docs.title: What's a Maestro Flow?
docs.text: The process that ties agents, robots, and people together. You already built the workers. Maestro decides who works when — and waits for the human. Orchestrates Calls your agent and your RPA process, and passes data between them. Humans in the loop Pauses for an approval in Action Center, then carries on. Observable Every run, every step, every input and output is visible after the fact.

docs.title: What the flow does
docs.text:
WHAT THE FLOW DOES Start 01 Manual trigger with one input: job_title Shortlist 02 Run the Coded Agent from Lab 1 Approve 03 The recruiter approves or rejects the shortlist in Action Center Register 04 On approval, run the RPA workflow from Lab 2 YOUR OBJECTIVES
  • 1 Prompt your coding agent to build the flow — it loads the uipath-maestro-flow skill.
  • 2 Let it discover your two processes in the folder before it builds anything.
  • 3 Validate and publish the flow.
  • 4 Run it end to end and approve the shortlist yourself.
Your building blocks: {YourName}JobMatchingAgent and {YourName}RegisterInUiBank in the CodingAgentsILT folder — or the trainer's DemoJobMatchingAgent and DemoRegisterInUiBank if yours didn't make it.

docs.title: The prompt
docs.text:
Your own componentsTrainer's processes

Use this whenever your agent from Lab 1 and your workflow from Lab 2 are published and work as expected.

Build a Maestro Flow called {YourName}RecruitmentPipeline, in a new local
folder named {YourName}RecruitmentPipeline, that runs the recruitment
pipeline end to end. Publish it to the CodingAgentsILT folder in Orchestrator.

1. Trigger: manual, with one input job_title (string)
2. Run the {YourName}JobMatchingAgent process with { job_title }
3. Create an approval task assigned to me that shows the job title and the
   three matches with first_name, last_name, score, and reason.
   Approve continues, Reject ends the flow
4. On Approve, run the {YourName}RegisterInUiBank process with
   in_CandidatesJson set to the agent's matches, serialized as a JSON string
5. End with outputs: the agent's job and the RPA's out_ResultsJson

Discover both processes in the CodingAgentsILT folder before you start, and
ask me before creating anything new. Validate the flow, publish it, and tell
me how to run it.

Use this only if your own agent or workflow isn't published or doesn't work as expected — for example, it fails when you run it, or its output doesn't match the contract. The trainer's DemoJobMatchingAgent and DemoRegisterInUiBank follow the same contract — see Resources.

Build a Maestro Flow called {YourName}RecruitmentPipeline, in a new local
folder named {YourName}RecruitmentPipeline, that runs the recruitment
pipeline end to end. Publish it to the CodingAgentsILT folder in Orchestrator.

1. Trigger: manual, with one input job_title (string)
2. Run the DemoJobMatchingAgent process with { job_title }
3. Create an approval task assigned to me that shows the job title and the
   three matches with first_name, last_name, score, and reason.
   Approve continues, Reject ends the flow
4. On Approve, run the DemoRegisterInUiBank process with
   in_CandidatesJson set to the agent's matches, serialized as a JSON string
5. End with outputs: the agent's job and the RPA's out_ResultsJson

Discover both processes in the CodingAgentsILT folder before you start, and
ask me before creating anything new. Validate the flow, publish it, and tell
me how to run it.

Only one of yours isn't working?

Keep the one that works. For example, if your agent works but your workflow doesn't, use {YourName}JobMatchingAgent in step 2 and DemoRegisterInUiBank in step 4.

docs.title: See the flow in Studio Web
docs.text:
Your coding agent builds the flow as a .flow file on your machine. To see it as a diagram, create a Flow in Studio Web and upload that file into it.

  1. Go to https://cloud.uipath.com/tpenlabs, select the InvokeWorkshop tenant, and open Studio Web.
  2. Select Create New, and under MAESTRO AUTOMATE choose Flow. Name it {YourName}RecruitmentPipeline.
  3. In the Explorer, right-click the Flow project and choose Import. Select the .flow file from your local {YourName}RecruitmentPipeline folder and select Open.
  4. The imported file opens in a new tab. The canvas shows every node and how they connect.

Flow under Maestro Automate, not Maestro Orchestrate

The menu lists Flow twice. Pick the one under MAESTRO AUTOMATE — that's the kind of flow your coding agent built. Don't use the one under MAESTRO ORCHESTRATE.

docs.title: What it builds
docs.text:
The flow your coding agent builds should look like this in Studio Web:

The finished {YourName}RecruitmentPipeline flow

Node What it does Manual trigger Starts the run with your job_title Run Job Matching Agent Calls your Coded Agent and gets back job and matches Prepare Approval Data A script step that formats the job title and the three matches for the approval task Approve Matches Creates the task in Action Center and waits. Approve and Reject lead to different branches. Register In UiBank On Approve, runs your RPA workflow with the matches as in_CandidatesJson Candidates Registered / Matches Rejected The two ways the run can end

Your layout and node names can differ a little — what matters is the same order of steps and the two branches after the approval.

Make changes in one place

The upload is a copy. Changes you make in Studio Web don't reach your local files, and changes your coding agent makes locally don't reach Studio Web. If your coding agent changes the flow, upload the .flow file again to see the new version.

docs.title: Run it end to end
docs.text:
1. Start the flow with job_title set to Forward Deployed Engineer — ask your coding agent to start it, or start it from Maestro in your tenant.
  2. Wait for the agent step to finish. The flow pauses on the approval.
  3. Open Action Center, find the task, read the shortlist, and approve it.
  4. Watch the RPA job run in Orchestrator. The robot registers the three candidates on UiBank.
  5. Open the finished run in Maestro and check the outputs: the JD and a status for each candidate.

What 'done' looks like

One Maestro run that starts from a job title and ends with registered candidates — with no manual step in between except the approval you designed in.

docs.title: Where it usually breaks
docs.text:
Symptom Likely cause Ask your coding agent to… Flow can't find a process The process isn't in the CodingAgentsILT folder yet List the processes in the folder and fix the name Robot step fails straight away in_CandidatesJson got an object, not a string Serialize the matches to a JSON string before passing them Robot registers people with blank fields The agent dropped candidate fields from matches Check the agent's output against the contract No task in Action Center The task is assigned to someone else Assign the approval to your user RPA job stays pending No robot is free in the folder Tell the trainer — robots are shared

Stuck? That's expected

Ask your coding agent to explain what it generated, check the run in Maestro and Orchestrator, and send the interesting failures our way with uip feedback send.

docs.title: Gotchas you'll hit
docs.text:
Things every team learns in the first month.

Gotcha What to do Trust but verify The agent is fast and confident. Always review generated XAML and run the eval set before publishing. Agree on the contract first Separate components built by separate prompts only fit together if the names and shapes are fixed up front. Pin your skill versions Skills evolve. Lock to a version in your project so behaviour doesn't shift under you. Context window matters On large projects the agent can miss context. Tell it which files to focus on, or use an AGENTS.md. Auth before everything Run uip login first. Skills can't deploy if the CLI session expired — this is the usual cause of "it just stopped working".

docs.title: What you built
docs.text:
One end-to-end recruitment pipeline:

# Component What it does 01 Coded Agent LangGraph agent. Generates a job description and shortlists the top 3 candidates. 02 RPA Workflow XAML workflow. Registers each candidate on UiBank and returns a status per candidate. 03 Maestro Flow Runs the agent, waits for the recruiter's approval in Action Center, then runs the robot.

All three were built with your coding agent, and they run as one process — in two 90-minute blocks.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
This week

  • Install the skills on your laptop and actually use them.
  • Run your pipeline with a different job title and see how the shortlist changes.

Next 30 days

  • Rebuild something you already maintain with a coding agent. Compare how long it took, and note where the agent needed correcting.
  • Write your own skill for a pattern your team repeats, so the agent gets it right without being told twice.
  • Push past the happy path: ask the agent for eval sets, error handling, and the deploy step you'd normally do by hand.

Ongoing

  • Bring your questions. No question is too basic, especially this early.
  • Tell us when something doesn't work. Run uip feedback send the moment a skill guesses wrong, a command fails, or a step takes three tries.
  • Say what you'd want next. The rough edges you report are what shape the next version of the skills and the CLI.

docs.title: Appendix: CLI cheat sheet
docs.text:
Commands you'll run every day with the uip CLI.

Command What it does When you'll use it uip skills install Install UiPath skills into your coding agent First-time setup, per project uip login Authenticate with your UiPath tenant Start of each session uipath new Scaffold a new Coded Agent project Starting a new agent uipath run Run the agent locally with input.json Testing during development uipath eval Run the evaluation set, score against expectations Before deploying uipath publish Pack and publish to your tenant Shipping uip feedback send Report a bug or a skill that guessed wrong Whenever something breaks

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
You've reached the end of the workshop

You've gone from setting up the uip CLI to building agents and orchestrating them in Maestro — with a coding agent doing the build work alongside you.

docs.title: Keep building
docs.text:
• Re-run the exercises against your own use cases and data.
  • Try a different coding agent (Cursor, Gemini CLI, Codex) with the same UiPath skills.
  • Extend a Maestro solution with an additional agent or human-in-the-loop step.

docs.text:
Everything you install before the workshop starts. Work through it top to bottom — each section verifies itself before you move on.

Do this before the session

Setup takes about 35 minutes on a clean machine, and some downloads are large. Get it done ahead of time so the session stays hands-on.

docs.title: 1. Prerequisites
docs.text:
Node.js (LTS) — required for the UiPath CLI and the React app build.

  1. Download the LTS version from nodejs.org
  2. Verify with node --version and npm --version

npm version must be 11.x.x

If npm --version returns a different version, upgrade it:

WindowsMac 
npm install --global npm@11

npm install -g npm@11

Python 3.10+ — required for coded agents.

  1. Download from python.org/downloads — on Windows, check Add Python to PATH during install
  2. Verify with python --version or python3 --version

.NET SDK 8.0 — required to build and run UiPath Studio projects.

  1. Download from dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet/8.0 — or on Mac, install via Homebrew: 
    brew install --cask dotnet-sdk
  2. Verify with dotnet --list-sdks — you should see 8.x.x in the output

Windows — make sure .NET is on your PATH

If dotnet is not recognised after install, add it to the PATH manually in PowerShell: 

$env:Path = "C:\Program Files\dotnet;$env:Path"
dotnet --list-sdks

UiPath Studio — required to open, run, and debug generated XAML workflows. Currently supported on Windows only; Mac support is coming soon.

  1. Download from uipath.com/start-trial
  2. Sign in with your UiPath account and verify Studio launches

Git — required for the UiPath skills marketplace. Try Method 1 first; if it doesn't work, use Method 2.

Method 1: winget (quickest)Method 2: Download the installer
  1. Open a terminal and run: 
    winget install --id Git.Git -e --source winget
  2. If prompted to accept terms, type Y and press Enter.
  3. Wait for "Successfully installed", then close the window.
  1. Go to git-scm.com/download/win — the 64-bit installer should download automatically.
  2. Run the downloaded file (e.g. Git-2.xx.x-64-bit.exe). Click Yes if Windows asks for admin permission.
  3. Click through the installer accepting all defaults. On the "Adjusting your PATH environment" screen, make sure the middle option is selected: "Git from the command line and also from 3rd-party software" — this is the default.
  4. Click Finish when done.

Required for both methods

PATH changes only take effect in new windows. Close every open terminal, then open a fresh Command Prompt and verify: 

git --version
You should see something like git version 2.45.1.windows.1.

docs.title: 2. Install a Coding Agent
docs.text:
Pick one — or install more than one:

Claude CodeCodexCursor 
npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code

Verify: claude --version

Claude Code installation error?

If the install fails with a scripts permission error, run: 

npm config set allow-scripts=@anthropic-ai/claude-code --location=user
Then run the install command again: 
npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code

npm permission errors on Mac?

A global install without write permissions is the usual cause. Point npm at a folder you own: 

mkdir -p ~/.npm-global
npm config set prefix ~/.npm-global
echo 'export PATH="$HOME/.npm-global/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.zshrc
source ~/.zshrc


npm install -g @openai/codex

Verify: codex --version

npm permission errors on Mac?

A global install without write permissions is the usual cause. Point npm at a folder you own: 

mkdir -p ~/.npm-global
npm config set prefix ~/.npm-global
echo 'export PATH="$HOME/.npm-global/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.zshrc
source ~/.zshrc

Cursor comes as an editor and as a terminal agent. Install both — you'll review generated files in the editor and run the agent from the terminal.

  1. Download and install the Cursor editor from cursor.com/downloads, then sign in.

  2. Install the Cursor CLI:

    Mac:

    curl https://cursor.com/install -fsS | bash

    Windows (PowerShell):

    irm 'https://cursor.com/install?win32=true' | iex

  3. Open a new terminal and sign in:

    cursor-agent login

Verify: cursor-agent --version

cursor-agent not found?

The installer puts the CLI in ~/.local/bin. Open a new terminal, or add that folder to your PATH.

docs.title: What's a Coding Agent?
docs.text:
Learn how coding agents work and what makes them useful for UiPath automation work.

A coding agent is an AI assistant that reads, writes, and reasons about code — not just autocompletes it. Instead of suggesting the next line, it understands a goal described in plain English, explores the codebase, makes decisions, and generates entire working components. You stay in control: you review what it builds, ask it to adjust, and iterate until it's right.

Several coding agents are available today, each with their own strengths:

  • Claude Code — Anthropic's CLI-based agent, runs in your terminal, deeply integrated with the file system. This is the one used in this exercise.
  • Codex CLI — OpenAI's command-line coding agent, similar terminal-first approach
  • Cursor — an IDE built around AI, tight editor integration with inline generation and multi-file context
  • Gemini CLI — Google's terminal agent, strong on reasoning and long context
  • GitHub Copilot Agent — embedded in VS Code and JetBrains, well suited for in-editor workflows

What makes coding agents especially powerful for UiPath work is the skill layer: by loading domain-specific knowledge about UiPath activities, APIs, and project conventions, the agent can generate production-ready automation code — not generic boilerplate. That's exactly what the UiPath skills in this exercise do.

docs.title: The Mental Model
docs.text:
Five concepts show up in every coding agent:

Concept What it is Tools Built-in actions the agent can take: read a file, run a bash command, search the web, edit code, etc. Skills Domain knowledge bundles the agent loads when it sees a matching task. Like a playbook for one thing. Commands Manual shortcuts you type: /commit, /test, /deploy. Triggered by you, not the agent. Hooks Run automatically at lifecycle events: before an edit, after a commit, on session start. Used for guardrails. Subagents Specialised workers spawned by the main agent. Used to parallelise or isolate complex tasks.

Plugins

A plugin is a package that bundles any of these together — like a Marketplace app for your coding agent. The UiPath skills used in this exercise are plugins.

docs.title: Tools, in practice
docs.text:
Claude Code's built-in tools are always available — no setup required:

Tool What it does Read Read any file in your project Edit / Write Modify or create files Bash Execute shell commands Glob / Grep Search across the codebase WebSearch / WebFetch Look things up online Task Spawn a subagent

Extension Tools (MCP)

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is the standard way to give your coding agent new tools without changing the agent itself.

  • GitHub MCP — read issues, open PRs
  • Atlassian MCP — Jira, Confluence
  • Slack MCP — read channels, post messages
  • Custom UiPath MCP — call Orchestrator, Maestro

docs.title: Skills, in practice
docs.text:
A skill is a folder — sitting in .claude/skills/ (or equivalent), with a SKILL.md inside.

Property What it means Discovered automatically The agent reads each SKILL.md's description. When your prompt matches, it loads the full skill on demand. More than just text Skills can bundle reference docs, code patterns, helper scripts, even compiled binaries the agent can run. Scoped permissions A skill declares which tools it's allowed to use. Bash access can be tightly controlled.

docs.title: What's in a SKILL.md file
docs.text:
Every skill is built around a single SKILL.md file. Here's what one looks like:

---
name: uipath-coded-agents
description: Scaffold, build, run, evaluate, and deploy UiPath coded agents...
allowed-tools: [Read, Edit, Bash(uip:*), Bash(uipath:*)]
---

# How to build a UiPath coded agent

When the user asks for a new coded agent:

1. Run `uipath new --framework langgraph`
2. Create agent.py following the pattern in references/
3. Add an evals/ folder with at least 5 test cases
4. Run `uipath eval` before deploying

## References
- references/sdk-methods.md
- references/langgraph-patterns.md

The file has four parts:

Part What it does Frontmatter Declares the skill's name, description, and which tools it's allowed to use. Discovery prompt The description field is what the agent matches against your request — this is how the skill gets loaded automatically. Instructions The body of the file: a step-by-step prompt the agent follows when the skill is active. References Paths to files in the skill folder the agent can read for deeper context — API docs, code patterns, example projects.

docs.title: Where UiPath fits in this picture
docs.text:
UiPath ships a plugin for Claude Code. It bundles skills, hooks, and references — giving the agent domain knowledge about UiPath products out of the box.

npm -g install @uipath/cli
uip skills install

The plugin contains three things:

What Details 10+ skills Domain knowledge for every UiPath product: uipath-agents, uipath-rpa, uipath-maestro-flow, uipath-platform, uipath-test, and more. 1 subagent uipath-project-discovery-agent — auto-runs on first contact with a UiPath project and builds context for the agent. Hooks & references Session-start nudges, activity docs, and allowlists for safe read-only commands.

docs.title: The UiPath skill catalog
docs.text:
The plugin includes skills for every part of the UiPath platform. Three of them drive the labs in this exercise:

Skill Description uipath-agents Scaffold, build, run, evaluate, and deploy coded agents (LangGraph, LlamaIndex, OpenAI Agents) uipath-rpa Generate and edit RPA workflows (XAML) for Studio Desktop with a discovery-first approach uipath-maestro-flow Create, validate, and debug UiPath Flow projects using the .flow JSON format uipath-solution Create and deploy solutions uipath-platform Auth, Orchestrator management, solution lifecycle, Integration Service, CLI tools uipath-test Generate, run, and maintain automated test suites for UiPath projects

Skills used in this exercise

The three skills in bold — uipath-agents, uipath-rpa, and uipath-maestro-flow — are the ones you'll use to build the recruitment pipeline.

docs.title: Agenda
docs.text:
One connected scenario, built end to end in two 90-minute blocks. No breaks, mostly hands-on.

Setup is not part of the session

Complete the Setup page before Block 1 starts. The clock starts with the coding agents intro — there's no time to install Node.js, Studio, or the skills during the session.

Block 1 — Coding agents and the Coded Agent · 90 min

Time Part Focus Format 0:00–0:20 💡 Intro Coding agents, tools, skills, plugins. Where the uip CLI fits. Presentation + live demo 0:20–0:25 ✅ Ready check Run uip login status and start your coding agent Hands-on 0:25–0:30 🧭 Scenario and contract The recruitment pipeline, its architecture, and the data each component passes on Presentation 0:30–1:20 🤖 Coded Agent Generate a JD, shortlist candidates, publish as a process Hands-on 1:20–1:30 💬 Checkpoint Compare shortlists. Confirm every agent is published. Discussion

Block 2 — The RPA workflow and the Maestro Flow · 90 min

Time Part Focus Format 0:00–0:30 ⚙️ RPA Workflow Register candidates on UiBank, publish as a process Hands-on 0:30–1:20 🔗 Maestro Flow Agent → approval in Action Center → robot. Run it end to end. Hands-on 1:20–1:30 🏁 Wrap-up What you built, gotchas, what to try next Discussion

How the timing holds up without breaks

  • The contract keeps the labs independent. Every component's inputs and outputs are fixed before you build it, so Lab 3 is wiring, not debugging.
  • Your coding agent's build time is your reading time. While it works, read the explanation sections of the lab.
  • Every lab has a fallback. The trainer publishes DemoJobMatchingAgent and DemoRegisterInUiBank in the shared folder. If your own component doesn't finish in its time box, use the trainer's in Lab 3 — you still finish the full pipeline.
